title: GeoJSON Area Calculator: Polygon Size in km²
description: Calculate the spherical area of GeoJSON polygons with the GeoJSON Area Calculator — square kilometres and acres from pasted geometry. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 0.01° × 0.01° test square drawn in New York measures 0.937 km² (231 acres) — not the 1.23 km² a flat map would claim, because longitude degrees are shorter there.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Area Calculator computes the approximate spherical area enclosed by GeoJSON polygons — in square kilometres and acres — directly from the geometry you paste. Read the total for every polygon in the file: parcels, districts and lakes measured on the sphere, not the flat lie of the screen.

A file claiming to hold a county should measure near the county’s known size. The area is the checksum geography provides free.
Service areas, protected zones and sales territories report in km² and acres — computed from the same geometry everyone is looking at.
Measure the same degree-square at the equator and at 60° — the two areas are the Mercator lecture, delivered by arithmetic.
A 1° × 1° square at the equator encloses about 12,300 km²; the same angular square at 60° encloses roughly half. Angular size is not ground size — this calculator reports the ground.

A park polygon with a lake cut out (an inner ring) measures land only — inner rings subtract by the ring-orientation rules of spherical area. Donut geography is handled as geography, not as a surprise.

popular_table.note: Areas are computed on the sphere with the standard ring algorithm (the one popularised by Mapbox’s geojson-area): accurate to well within a percent for ordinary polygons — planning-grade, not survey-grade.

faq: How accurate is the spherical method?

For typical parcels and regions, within a fraction of a percent of ellipsoidal truth. Legal boundaries and cadastral areas come from licensed survey work — this is the measurement for analysis, reporting and checking.
Square kilometres headline; acres convert at 1 km² = 247.105 acres, hectares at exactly 100 per km². US audiences get acres, European audiences hectares and km² — all from the same geometry.
GeoJSON rings should repeat the first point at the end. The calculator treats rings as closed figures; a badly unclosed ring in source data is a data bug worth fixing at the source.
Robust implementations read winding to tell outer rings from holes (the RFC 7946 right-hand rule). Reversed files can produce nonsense totals — a negative or absurd area is the tell.
Polygons crossing ±180° (Fiji, Russia’s far east) can compute wildly if the ring jumps the seam naively. Split such polygons at the meridian for sane areas.
A bowtie ring has no honest area — the algorithm returns a number, but geometry that crosses itself is broken input. Fix the ring, then measure.
Ignored — area is a surface measure of the lon/lat outline; the third element rides along unmeasured.
